subtopics.title: Group data into histograms
subtopics.exposition: Grouping continuous quantitative data means subdividing the full range of values into a few sub-ranges. Each continuous value is assigned to the sub-range, or class, within which it falls; this changes the data set from continuous to discrete. A histogram is a collection of rectangles, where the base of each rectangle (on the x-axis) covers the values in the range associated with it. The sub-ranges must not overlap and must cover the entire range of the data set. To group data, define a set of ranges and then count how many of the data fall inside each range. To tabulate grouped data, count the number of values in each range; for the 30 learners' heights the counts are 7, 5, 7, 9 and 2 for the ranges 130 ≤ h < 140 up to 170 ≤ h < 180. When drawing the histogram, the number of rectangles equals the number of ranges (5 ranges give 5 rectangles). When drawing the histogram, the base of each rectangle is defined by its range and the height of each rectangle is determined by the count in its range. Ranges such as 130 ≤ h < 140 and 140 ≤ h < 150 do not overlap because each range starts where the previous one ended.

subtopics.title: Read and check histograms
subtopics.exposition: In a histogram, the height of a rectangle corresponds to the number of values in its range, so the count for a range is read from the height of its rectangle.

subtopics.title: Estimate centre of grouped data
subtopics.exposition: The modal group is the group that has the highest number of data values. The median group is the central group when the groups are arranged in order. Grouping changes the measures of central tendency because each datum is treated as if it occurred at the centre of the range in which it was placed. To estimate measures of central tendency from grouped data, assume that the values are grouped at the centre of each range. In the grouped data set each value is placed at the centre of its range, and the number of times each centre value is repeated equals the count in that range. For the 30 learners' heights before grouping, the mean is 151.8 and the median is 152. After grouping the learners' heights, with each value at the centre of its range, the mean is 153, the median is 155 and the mode is 165. For grouped data one can also just give the modal group and the median group.

claims.claim: Grouping continuous quantitative data means subdividing the full range of values into a few sub-ranges.
Each continuous value is assigned to the sub-range, or class, within which it falls; this changes the data set from continuous to discrete.
To group data, define a set of ranges and then count how many of the data fall inside each range.
The sub-ranges must not overlap and must cover the entire range of the data set.
Ranges such as 130 ≤ h < 140 and 140 ≤ h < 150 do not overlap because each range starts where the previous one ended.
A histogram is a collection of rectangles, where the base of each rectangle (on the x-axis) covers the values in the range associated with it.
To tabulate grouped data, count the number of values in each range; for the 30 learners' heights the counts are 7, 5, 7, 9 and 2 for the ranges 130 ≤ h < 140 up to 170 ≤ h < 180.
When drawing the histogram, the number of rectangles equals the number of ranges (5 ranges give 5 rectangles).
When drawing the histogram, the base of each rectangle is defined by its range and the height of each rectangle is determined by the count in its range.
In a histogram, the height of a rectangle corresponds to the number of values in its range, so the count for a range is read from the height of its rectangle.
A histogram makes it easy to see in which range most of the values are located and gives an overview of the distribution of the values in the data set.
With grouped data the estimates of central tendency change, because some information is lost when each value is placed in a range.
If only the grouped data is available, the measured values are not known to the same accuracy as before.
To estimate measures of central tendency from grouped data, assume that the values are grouped at the centre of each range.
In the grouped data set each value is placed at the centre of its range, and the number of times each centre value is repeated equals the count in that range.
Grouping changes the measures of central tendency because each datum is treated as if it occurred at the centre of the range in which it was placed.
For the 30 learners' heights before grouping, the mean is 151.8 and the median is 152.
The mode of the ungrouped heights is 132, but there are problems with computing the mode of continuous quantitative data.
After grouping the learners' heights, with each value at the centre of its range, the mean is 153, the median is 155 and the mode is 165.
The grouped mode of 165 is a better estimate of the mode than the ungrouped mode, since the grouping showed in which range the learners' heights were clustered.
For grouped data one can also just give the modal group and the median group.
The modal group is the group that has the highest number of data values.
The median group is the central group when the groups are arranged in order.
